fit_paragraphs.text: Prof. Carpuat's CLIP Lab works at the intersection of multilingual NLP, speech, and human-centered evaluation [advisor:Marine Carpuat] — exactly the three axes of my PhD plan. Her group's XLAVS-R work on cross-lingual audio-visual speech representation [paper:W4402684056] connects directly to my course project on a wav2vec2-style model for Tamil radio audio [lib:cv]. The work on LLM post-editing of machine translation with error annotations [paper:W4401042399] resonates with my interest in evaluation that goes beyond surface accuracy [lib:interests]. Most concretely, the CHI 2025 study on generative AI design for non-native speakers [paper:W4409736318] mirrors questions I keep returning to: what does a model actually need to do to serve a Tamil–English code-switcher [lib:interests], and how do we measure it?

Prof. Rudinger's work on evaluation methodology for LLMs [advisor:Rachel Rudinger] speaks directly to my concern that translated English benchmarks miss what multilingual users need [lib:interests]. Her ACL 2025 paper on fixing multiple-choice evaluation with LLMs [paper:W4412886673] raises methodological questions I faced firsthand: when I tested open 7B models on code-switched Tamil–English inputs, the evaluation setup itself constrained what failures I could even detect [lib:cv]. Her ACL 2024 paper on whether LLMs discriminate in hiring [paper:W4402671226] also shows rigorous probing of model behavior in culturally situated contexts — a lens I want to apply to Indian-language NLP. I would be glad to contribute the low-resource multilingual side to her evaluation research program [lib:interests].

Prof. Wiegreffe's research on mechanistic interpretability and the faithfulness of natural language explanations [advisor:Sarah Wiegreffe] connects to a question I cannot yet answer about my own results: why do open 7B models drop 18–26 points on Tamil–English code-switched inputs [lib:cv]? Her 2024 BlackBoxNLP paper questioning what 'mechanistic' even means [paper:W4404784049] signals careful thinking about what interpretability tools actually reveal — exactly the rigor I would want when diagnosing failures in multilingual models. While her current work is not focused on low-resource languages [advisor:Sarah Wiegreffe], I see a productive overlap between her interpretability methodology and my evaluation interests [lib:interests], and I am curious whether her tools can illuminate cross-lingual representation gaps.

sop.text:
I am applying to the PhD program in Computer Science to work on multilingual NLP, specifically making large language models genuinely useful for the hundreds of millions of people who speak Indian languages but are poorly served by today's models [lib:interests].

My starting point was a concrete failure. In early 2025, working with Prof. S. Venkatesan at NIT Trichy, I built a Tamil–English code-switched evaluation set of 2,400 sentences and tested two open 7B models on it [lib:cv]. Both lost 18–26 points relative to their monolingual Tamil performance [lib:cv]. People in Chennai do not address a chatbot in clean monolingual Tamil; they switch mid-sentence. That gap became my first-author paper at a Student Research Workshop at an ACL-family conference in 2026 [lib:cv], and it reshaped how I think about the field: evaluation, not just training data, is a central place where multilingual NLP is broken [lib:interests].

During my summer 2026 internship at Microsoft Research India, mentored by Dr. Anjali Mehra, I worked on the adaptation side of the same problem [lib:cv]. Extending a SentencePiece vocabulary with 6,000 Kannada tokens cut average token count per sentence by 41% and improved downstream QA F1 by 3.4 points at the same fine-tuning budget [lib:cv]. The implication was clear: targeted, cheap changes to the tokenizer can matter as much as expensive fine-tuning runs [lib:cv]. That observation now anchors one of my core PhD directions: parameter-efficient and data-efficient adaptation of LLMs to low-resource Indian languages [lib:interests].

A third thread runs through a Spring 2026 course project in Speech Processing, where I trained a wav2vec2-style model on 40 hours of Tamil radio audio and reached 31% WER on a held-out set [lib:cv]. For many Indian languages, substantially more data exists in spoken form than in text [lib:interests]. Building models that can learn from audio and transfer across modalities is not a separate research program from my NLP work — it is a prerequisite for serving real users.

Putting these together, my PhD research agenda has three parts: (1) parameter-efficient and data-efficient adaptation of LLMs to low-resource languages, including tokenizer redesign and PEFT methods [lib:interests]; (2) evaluation frameworks that measure code-switching, cultural grounding, and faithfulness rather than performance on translated English benchmarks [lib:interests]; and (3) speech-text models for languages where data is primarily spoken [lib:interests].

At UMD, Prof. Marine Carpuat's CLIP Lab is the natural center of gravity for this work [advisor:Marine Carpuat]. Her group's research on cross-lingual audio-visual speech representation [paper:W4402684056], LLM-guided post-editing of machine translation [paper:W4401042399], and the design of generative AI tools for non-native speakers [paper:W4409736318] each address a different facet of the problem I want to solve. I am also drawn to Prof. Rachel Rudinger's work on LLM evaluation methodology [advisor:Rachel Rudinger]; her recent paper interrogating the structure of multiple-choice evaluation [paper:W4412886673] raises exactly the methodological concerns I ran into when designing my Tamil–English benchmark. Prof. Sarah Wiegreffe's mechanistic interpretability research [advisor:Sarah Wiegreffe], particularly her careful thinking about what interpretability tools actually reveal [paper:W4404784049], offers tools I want to use to understand why multilingual models fail rather than simply documenting that they do.

I hold a CGPA of 9.21/10 at NIT Tiruchirappalli, placing me in the top 5% of my department [lib:profile]. I have served as a teaching assistant for a 120-student machine learning course [lib:cv] and have organized my department's NLP reading group since 2025 [lib:cv]. I received the Institute Merit Scholarship in 2024, 2025, and 2026 [lib:cv]. I expect to graduate in May 2027 and am applying for Fall 2027 entry [lib:profile].

emails.subject: Prospective PhD student interested in multilingual NLP and speech-text models — Fall 2027
emails.body:
Dear Prof. Carpuat,

I am a final-year B.Tech student at NIT Tiruchirappalli applying to UMD CS for Fall 2027, and I wanted to ask whether you are planning to admit PhD students this cycle.

My research so far has focused on two problems your group also works on. For my undergraduate thesis, I built a Tamil–English code-switched evaluation set and showed that open 7B models lose 18–26 points versus monolingual Tamil baselines [lib:cv]. At Microsoft Research India this past summer, I extended a SentencePiece vocabulary with 6,000 Kannada tokens, cutting token count by 41% and improving QA F1 by 3.4 points [lib:cv].

I was especially engaged by your group's XLAVS-R paper on cross-lingual audio-visual speech representation learning (Han et al., ACL 2024) [paper:W4402684056], which connects directly to a course project where I trained a small speech model on Tamil radio audio [lib:cv].

I would be glad to share my CV and first-author workshop paper if helpful. Please let me know if you have space in your group.

Best regards,
Priya Raman

emails.subject: Prospective PhD student interested in LLM evaluation methodology — Fall 2027
emails.body:
Dear Prof. Rudinger,

I am a final-year B.Tech student at NIT Tiruchirappalli applying to UMD CS for Fall 2027, and your website indicates you are admitting PhD students this cycle [advisor:Rachel Rudinger] — I wanted to introduce myself.

My work centers on evaluation: I built a Tamil–English code-switched benchmark and found that standard monolingual evaluation misses large failure modes in open 7B models [lib:cv]. That experience made me attuned to the structural problems in how we assess LLMs, which is why I found your ACL 2025 paper — "Which of These Best Describes Multiple Choice Evaluation with LLMs?" (Balepur, Rudinger, Boyd-Graber, ACL 2025) [paper:W4412886673] — directly relevant to choices I had to make designing my own benchmark.

I am particularly interested in bringing a low-resource multilingual perspective to your evaluation methodology work [lib:interests].

I would be happy to share my CV and first-author workshop paper. Thank you for your time.

Best regards,
Priya Raman

emails.subject: Prospective PhD student interested in mechanistic interpretability for multilingual models — Fall 2027
emails.body:
Dear Prof. Wiegreffe,

I am a final-year B.Tech student at NIT Tiruchirappalli applying to UMD CS for Fall 2027, and I wanted to ask whether you are planning to take PhD students this cycle.

My research documents performance failures in open LLMs on Tamil–English code-switched inputs — an 18–26 point drop versus monolingual baselines [lib:cv] — but I cannot yet explain mechanistically why those failures occur. Your 2024 BlackBoxNLP paper with Naomi Saphra, "Mechanistic?" (Saphra and Wiegreffe, BlackBoxNLP @ EMNLP 2024) [paper:W4404784049], resonates with me precisely because it asks what interpretability tools actually reveal, which is the rigor I would want before applying them to cross-lingual representation gaps [lib:interests].

While I know your group's focus is not primarily on low-resource languages [advisor:Sarah Wiegreffe], I think the methodological questions overlap, and I would welcome a conversation.

I am happy to share my CV and workshop paper.

Best regards,
Priya Raman
